name: Muno
catalog_citation: Rönchen, Philipp. 2025. 'First notes on Muno (Papua New Guinea)'. NUSA 77-78: 1-37. doi:10.15026/0002001225; open PDF at https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/2001225/files/muno_first_notes.pdf
catalog_quote: Muno appears to not be tonal. Stress in Muno is at present not well understood. It appears that Muno mostly has lexical stress; when uttered in isolation some two-syllabic words consistently have stress on the first and some have stress on the second syllable. Tri-syllabic non-inflected words often have stress on the third syllable. Inflection or the presence of clitics can sometimes shift stress: Compare tanu [’ta.nu] ‘we came’ with tanua [ta.’nu.a] ‘we came and’ as it occurs in Example 48.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote and locator verified verbatim in the PDF we hold (p. 7, sec. 2.5). The deciding source is a 2025 open-access first-notes sketch, thin on prosody (two hedged sentences, explicitly 'not well understood'), but it is the best and effectively the only published description of this near-undocumented isolate: Glottolog 5.1 has no grammar/sketch/phonology for guri1248, and Baron 1983 (downloaded now) is silent on Guriaso stress. The catalog's 'lexical, non-strict' coding with the the primary-stress rule caveats (trisyllables often final, clitic-driven rightward shift, author flags as preliminary) faithfully reflects the source. Not 'well-sourced' because the source itself disclaims a settled analysis and one unpublished SIL phonology (Edmondson 2022) remains unread; not 'at-risk' because nothing seen suggests a different coding. no reclassification; keep the caution that the analysis is preliminary.
